title: Gideon and the Aftermath
premise: After their father's funeral, nonbinary archivist Zephyrine Thornbury sorts through a house full of unsent letters and discovers a song playing on local radio that their father wrote and never recorded—a song he claimed was destroyed decades ago. Following the melody back to the coastal commune where he once lived, Zephyrine uncovers a community that survived by erasing him: he had been their songwriter, their conscience, and finally their scapegoat when his lyrics exposed the founder's abuses of power. As the commune's aging founders close ranks and the song's co-writer, now dying, seeks absolution, Zephyrine must choose between publishing the truth that will give them a lineage and destroying it to protect the only family their father ever chose. In the end, Zephyrine records the song themselves, sings it back to the town that silenced him, and claims both the inheritance of grief and the right to be seen.
about_author: Felix Ravensworth is the pen name of a former funeral-home archivist who spent a decade cataloging the belongings of the unclaimed dead. Their fiction examines what families preserve, what they bury, and who is left to do the digging.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Silence
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, cataloging their father Edmund's house after the funeral, records every unspoken thing in a notebook: the locked drawer, the absence of photographs before 1985, the piano with its strings removed. Third-person limited POV. The beat is controlled grief, order imposed on loss, until the notebook itself becomes a character of avoidance.

chapters.title: A Song That Never Was
chapters.summary: Driving home, Zephyrine hears a radio broadcast of a local-history segment featuring a demo tape: a song Edmund wrote for the Halcyon Cove commune and never recorded, performed by a voice Zephyrine doesn't recognize. The station credits 'E. Thornbury, 1983.' Zephyrine's careful inventory collapses. POV stays with Zephyrine; the beat is vertigo—the past refusing to stay catalogued.

chapters.title: Halcyon Cove
chapters.summary: Zephyrine travels to the decaying coastal commune, now half-ruin and half-retirement community, and is met with warm, practiced hospitality that curdles into deflection the moment Edmund's name surfaces. POV Zephyrine. The beat is the uncanny charm of institutions built on a story everyone has agreed to tell.

chapters.title: The Founder's Chair
chapters.summary: Zephyrine meets Marguerite Voss, the commune's aging founder, who receives them like a returning child and speaks of Edmund in the past tense of a traitor. Marguerite reveals she knew of the funeral and sent nothing. POV Zephyrine. The beat is the first taste of power's polish—generosity deployed as control.

chapters.title: What the Strings Remembered
chapters.summary: In the commune's archive, Zephyrine finds the removed piano strings from their father's house, labeled with a 1985 date, and a scrapbook of clippings about a scandal the commune calls 'the Difficult Year.' POV shifts briefly to Marguerite, who remembers editing the past and feels no guilt, only stewardship. The beat is dread sharpening into evidence.

chapters.title: The Dying Co-Writer
chapters.summary: Zephyrine tracks down Wren Okonjo, Edmund's co-writer, now hospice-bound, who plays the demo's original recording and begins to confess: the song was written to expose Marguerite's exploitation of commune laborers, and Edmund was expelled to keep it silent. Wren's POV. The beat is a deathbed urgency—truth handed over like a hot coal.

chapters.title: The Difficult Year
chapters.summary: Wren's testimony unspools the full history: the exploited workers, the song as whistleblowing, the vote to erase Edmund, and Wren's own silence in exchange for staying. Zephyrine learns their father's invisibility was manufactured, and that they were raised inside its aftermath. POV alternates Wren and Zephyrine. The beat is fury and recognition—identity reframed as inheritance.

chapters.title: An Offer of Belonging
chapters.summary: Marguerite, learning Zephyrine has the tape, offers them Edmund's old cottage, a place on the council, and a family—provided the song stays unrecorded. Zephyrine, starved for belonging, genuinely considers it. POV Zephyrine. The beat is temptation rendered honestly: corruption rarely looks like corruption from inside.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: In the ruined music hall where Edmund wrote the song, Zephyrine records it themselves, voice cracking, Wren listening by phone from the hospice. Marguerite's allies arrive to stop them and find the commune's younger residents—descendants of the exploited—standing witness instead. POV Zephyrine. The beat is the climax: an act of witness that cannot be unsung.

chapters.title: Everything Unsaid, Said
chapters.summary: The recording airs; Marguerite's reign of curated memory ends not with ruin but with reckoning, as the commune votes to tell its history whole. Zephyrine buries the notebook in Edmund's grave, having said everything, and stays—not in the offered cottage but in a house of their own choosing. POV Zephyrine. The beat is resolution: belonging earned by truth, identity claimed aloud.
